output.rationale: The hypothesis focuses on comparing oversampling (SMOTE) versus class weighting in logistic regression for minority-class recall in imbalanced tabular datasets. To ensure generalizability beyond single datasets and model types, we select two publicly available, imbalanced datasets—breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10—both with a minority class reduced to 10% of the majority, matching the imbalanced condition in the gap G4. The control condition uses class weighting (as in E1), which is claimed to yield higher recall (0.66 vs. 0.17), while the treatment applies oversampling (via SMOTE) to the same logistic regression model. This design directly tests the hypothesis under a broader scope (G1), includes a single model and method comparison (G2), and allows for statistical validation via paired Wilcoxon test (G4). Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness, and three random seeds ensure reproducibility and variance estimation. The choice of metrics is limited to 'minority_recall' as the dependent variable, aligning with the hypothesis. The paired Wilcoxon test is appropriate because it compares two related samples (same model, different conditions) under non-normality assumptions, which is common in imbalanced classification.

The control condition (logistic_regression+class_weight) represents a standard, commonly used approach for handling imbalance, allowing us to benchmark against alternative oversampling methods. The treatment conditions test ADASYN, SMOTE, and borderline SMOTE, as specified in the hypothesis. F1-score is the primary metric (dependent variable) to evaluate performance, as per the hypothesis. A paired Wilcoxon test is used to compare the F1-scores between the control and each treatment, as it is appropriate for non-parametric comparisons of paired observations. Five-fold cross-validation ensures stability and reduces variance, and three random seeds are used to ensure reproducibility and to assess the consistency of results across different data splits.
